comments.location_title: Lesson 10 · Read convergence pictures without being misled
comments.author: Nechshadimov
comments.text: The most useful view for me: 3D surface of the solution x[k] with a fixed colour scale. On 128×128 with 8×8 subdomains, the hill without coarse correction grew slowly (peak 30 → 395 → 1199 at iterations 1, 10, 40, about 50 iterations to full height). With balanced coarse correction it had the right height already at iteration 1. This showed me why the coarse correction reduces iterations better than any explanation.

comments.location_title: Lesson 10 · Read convergence pictures without being misled
comments.author: Nechshadimov
comments.text: The absolute residual 3D surface with "Rescale each iteration" looked like random spikes and I could not tell what it meant. I also first thought the slider was a physical heating process, not solver iterations. Suggestion: recommend starting with the solution x at a fixed scale, and say next to the slider that frames are iterations, not time.

comments.location_title: Lesson 11 · Find the parallel break-even point: MPI and GPU (if available)
comments.author: Nechshadimov
comments.text: Weak scaling with 64×64 per subdomain, one rank per subdomain, ASM+IC+CG, h=2: from 1 to 64 subdomains solve time grew ×47 without coarse correction, and ×15 with balanced Cx=Cy=2·Px. Iterations explain part of it (52 → 579 vs 39 → 135), but time per iteration also grew about 4×. The Lab does not report communication time separately, so I could not tell where that time went. A separate communication timing would help.

comments.location_title: Lesson 1 · From a physical field to a system of equations
comments.author: Nechshadimov
comments.text: When I first opened the lab I felt like I was sitting in an airplane cockpit. Over time it became clearer, but not completely, and it took me quite a lot of time to understand things. I have built many user interfaces, mostly built either specialised tools for people who already know the domain, or very simple things anyone with a computer can use intuitively. I think this lab belongs to the first type, so some interface complexity cannot be avoided. I am not an interface designer, so I cannot suggest anything concrete to make the interface more friendly, but maybe AI could suggest how to do it better :) Or maybe it does not need to be simplified at all, so that students have to dig deeper into the material.

comments.location_title: Lesson 12 · Build, critique and share a numerical argument
comments.author: Nechshadimov
comments.text: I used this lesson's approach for the weak-scaling homework: write the hypothesis first, change one thing at a time, keep everything else fixed, use a warm-up run plus 3 timed repeats and report the median. It made the comparison of coarse settings clean, and it helped me separate what I measured from what I only guessed, for example why the time per iteration grew about 4×. One practical difficulty: I ran 112 jobs by clicking Run one by one. A "repeat this configuration N times" option would save a lot of clicking.
